picks.style: greek choral ode, kithara and aulos, layered voices, soaring, expansive, wind-borne
picks.why: The eagle slicing the deep air on golden wings while thin-voiced birds crouch — the cleanest, grandest passage here.

picks.style: greek choral narrative ode, lyre and low drum, solo voice with choral answers, tense then transfigured, slow release
picks.why: Croesus on the pyre, Zeus quenching the golden flame with a rain-cloud, Apollo carrying the old man to the Hyperboreans.

picks.style: underworld lament, single aulos over a deep drone, hollow male voice, slow, ghostly, tear-struck
picks.why: Meleager's shade telling how his mother burned the log — and the only time Heracles ever wept.

picks.style: greek sea-chorus, lyre and light frame drum, layered female voices, rowing pulse, bright, hopeful
picks.why: 'O swift Phoenician ship of Sidon... mother of the oar, leader of the lovely dancing of dolphins' — a sailing song outright.

picks.style: greek choral threnody, solo aulos and soft kithara, mournful female voices, slow, trilling, keening
picks.why: The nightingale summoned from her leafy haunts to help carry the lament — one of Euripides' loveliest openings.

picks.style: greek tragic chorus, lyre over a low drone, massed female voices, incantatory, sorrowing, ceremonial
picks.why: Zeus shining through the air on the wings of a snow-white swan, and the doubled 'fated, fated' of Helen's life.

picks.style: roman canticum turned reflective, single tibia and soft strings, warm female voice, unhurried, candid, bittersweet
picks.why: The courtesan telling the good girl why virtue is possible for her and not for us — the play's most honest speech.

picks.style: roman comic canticum, tibia and plucked lyre, quick bright tenor, restless, wry
picks.why: 'What partial judges are all fathers' — and the vow that if he ever has a son he will be an indulgent father.

picks.style: roman stage monologue, low tibia and hand drum, weathered baritone, measured, rueful
picks.why: 'That they can see and judge of other men's affairs better than their own' — the whole play's moral in one line.

picks.style: scottish pastoral nocturne, fiddle and guitar over a soft drone, warm baritone, slow, moonlit, hushed
picks.why: The silver empress of the night, the limpid pool, the low-wheeling bat — a complete evening in four quatrains.

picks.style: border ballad, harp and low fiddle, plain female voice, modal, steady, mournful
picks.why: 'I come — I come, where bow nor spear shall more disturb our loves' — the ballad's death-scene, in true ballad metre.

picks.style: elegiac air, cello and piano, low male voice, slow, bare, aching
picks.why: 'For thou art gone — my guide, my friend, oh where' — grief measured against the hills and the sainted well.

picks.style: latin epic recitation, low strings and driving frame drum, urgent male voice, gathering, headlong, storm-lit
picks.why: An unbroken chain of similes — wolves under cloud, the skimming sea-bird, and the runaway chariots that end it.

picks.style: roman elegiac song, lyre and soft flute, grave tenor, slow, valedictory, evening
picks.why: 'Pale death with equal foot knocks at the poor man's door', closing on the unhitching of the steaming horses.

picks.style: german kinderlied, music box and simple piano, light child's soprano, gentle, lilting, tender
picks.why: A child's song about her doll in its cradle, ending 'I'm just as rich as you' — complete, innocent, and singable in either language.

picks.style: greek proverb-song, lyre and light hand drum, wry male voice, steady, aphoristic, companionable
picks.why: Only candidate, but it opens on a finished rhyming poem: old men with old, boys with boys, and the unlucky telling the unlucky.

picks.style: french romantic chanson, solo piano and cello, low male voice, slow, desolate, hearth-cold
picks.why: Only candidate; the silent spinning-wheel and the old man warming pale hands over smoke at an empty hearth.
